einstellungen.text: You're sure of it. That word was on the list.
Two days before your exhibition, you test the second station on yourself.
Eda reads you fifteen words for the station. Slowly. Then you have to write them all down.
Bed. Pillow. Dream. Blanket. Tired. Yawn. It all kind of fits together. Like a long evening.
Your marker squeaks across the paper. It smells like glue and sunshine.
You've got fourteen words. You grin. Almost perfect.
You read. Bed, pillow, dream … and sleep. Definitely sleep.
Eda doesn't say a word. She lays the original list next to yours.
The word sleep isn't on the original. Anywhere.
Your stomach drops. You heard it. In Eda's voice. You'd swear to it.
In studies from nineteen ninety-five, people confidently remembered fitting words that were never shown.
That doesn't mean all memories are wrong. Just that feeling sure doesn't always mean being right.
You pin your sheet to the wall. Your mistake becomes the example.
You count again. Your sure memory has one word more than the original.
